externalCodePrefixes.summary: Python type errors in template expressions and c-* values, such as a value of the wrong type for a component input. They come from ty, the Python type checker Citry runs. The part after citry.python. is ty's rule name, and the message is ty's.

TypeScript errors in component JavaScript and Vue expressions, such as a wrong argument type, an unknown member, or a wrong number of arguments. The part after citry.typescript. is TypeScript's error number, such as ts2322, and the message is TypeScript's. When one of Citry's own diagnostics already reports the same mistake, Citry shows only its own.

diagnostics.title: Invalid template syntax
diagnostics.summary: The template has a syntax mistake, such as an unclosed element or an unfinished expression. Citry cannot read the template, so it does not render.
diagnostics.when: The parser finds malformed markup, an incomplete expression, or another syntax error. Only the first syntax error in a template is reported.
diagnostics.fix: Correct the template at the reported position. The message says what the parser expected there.

messages.default: {detail}

diagnostics.title: Invalid template value
diagnostics.summary: Citry was given a value it cannot parse as a template. This is usually not a mistake in your template text.
diagnostics.when: A parser API receives a value it cannot turn into template source, for example when an extension that adds its own template syntax reports positions that do not fit the template.
diagnostics.fix: If an extension adds its own template syntax, update it or report the message to its authors. Otherwise, report the message as a Citry bug.

messages.default: {detail}

diagnostics.title: Template parser setup failed
diagnostics.summary: Citry could not set up the template parser for your application, so it cannot check this template.
diagnostics.when: The tag rules that your application or its extensions add to the parser cannot be built or applied.
diagnostics.fix: Read the message for the rule that failed, and fix the application or extension that defines it.

messages.default: {detail}

diagnostics.title: Unknown template variable
diagnostics.summary: A template reads a variable that nothing provides, often because of a typo. Rendering then fails with a KeyError.
diagnostics.when: A name in {{ ... }} or in a c-* attribute is not in the component's template data, a c-for or c-fill binding around it, template_globals, or the declared template_variables. In a template that several components share, every one of them must provide the name.
diagnostics.fix: Correct the name, or add it to the data that template_data() returns. If template_data() builds its result in a way Citry cannot read, such as by calling a helper function, list every key it returns in Lint.template_data_keys. If another integration provides the name, declare it in template_variables, or change rule_unknown_template_variable.

messages.closed: Template variable '{name}' is not available in this template.
messages.allow-extra: Template variable '{name}' is not declared. It may be supplied dynamically.
messages.unknown: Template variable '{name}' is not declared. Citry could not determine whether it is supplied dynamically.

examples.title: Unknown name in a dynamic attribute

diagnostics.title: Key missing from template_data_keys
diagnostics.summary: A component's template_data() returns a key that its Lint.template_data_keys does not list, so the list no longer names every key the method returns.
diagnostics.when: A component declares Lint.template_data_keys, and its template_data() writes a key as a literal, such as {"title": ...} or data["title"] = ..., that the list leaves out.
diagnostics.fix: Add the key to Lint.template_data_keys, or stop returning it.

messages.default: template_data() returns '{name}', but Lint.template_data_keys does not list it. Add '{name}' to the list so it names every key the method returns.

examples.title: A key the list leaves out

diagnostics.title: Unknown component
diagnostics.summary: A component tag names a component that your application does not register, often because of a typo. The template fails to render.
diagnostics.when: A <c-*> tag names no component in the selected application or library, counting built-in names and aliases.
diagnostics.fix: Correct the tag name, or register the component with the application that Citry loaded.

parameters.tag: Authored component tag, including the c- prefix.

messages.default: Component <{tag}> is not registered.

diagnostics.title: Invalid <c-mark> tag
diagnostics.summary: A <c-mark> tag, which marks part of a component that an event handler can replace, has no usable name, an extra attribute, or content it does not accept.
diagnostics.when: A <c-mark> tag has no name attribute, a dynamic or invalid name, any other attribute, or a named fill.
diagnostics.fix: Give the marker one literal name that starts with a letter and contains only letters, digits, _ or -. Remove other attributes and named fills.

messages.dynamic: Marker name must be a static literal.
messages.missing: Marker requires a literal name attribute.
messages.extra: Marker accepts only its name attribute.
messages.named_fill: Marker accepts only its default slot.

diagnostics.title: Alpine attribute on an HTML element
diagnostics.summary: An HTML element still has an Alpine x-* attribute, such as x-data or x-on:click. Citry uses Vue, so nothing reads it and it does nothing.
diagnostics.when: An Alpine directive name, such as x-data, x-on:click, or x-intersect, sits on an HTML element or <c-element>, including inside nested templates. Other x-* names, such as x-webkit-airplay, are ordinary HTML. Component tags are not checked, because an x-* attribute there is a Python keyword argument. x-cloak is reported as citry.template.alpine-cloak.
diagnostics.fix: Move the state into js_data() or $component, and write the listener in its Vue form, such as @click. If another library on the page reads x-* attributes, set rule_alpine_attribute to "ignore".

parameters.name: Attribute name as written in the template.

messages.default: '{name}' is an Alpine attribute. Citry uses Vue, so nothing reads it. Replace it with its Vue form, or set rule_alpine_attribute to 'ignore' if a library on the page reads '{name}'.

diagnostics.title: x-cloak hides an element for good
diagnostics.summary: An HTML element still has x-cloak. Nothing removes it, so a [x-cloak] CSS rule hides the element for good.
diagnostics.when: x-cloak, in any letter case, sits on an HTML element or <c-element>, including inside nested templates. Component tags are not checked.
diagnostics.fix: Delete x-cloak and its [x-cloak] CSS rule. The HTML from the server already shows the content.

messages.default: Nothing in Citry removes 'x-cloak', so a '[x-cloak]' CSS rule keeps this element hidden. Delete 'x-cloak' and its '[x-cloak]' rule; the server-rendered HTML already shows the content.

diagnostics.title: HTML attribute value the browser does not accept
diagnostics.summary: An HTML attribute that accepts only certain keywords, such as draggable or type, has another value, or a boolean attribute such as disabled has a value other than empty or its own name, which still turns it on. The browser raises no error either way.
diagnostics.when: The value is not one of the keywords the HTML Standard lists for that attribute on that element. A boolean attribute, such as disabled or required, is on whenever it is present, so any value other than the empty string or the attribute's own name is reported, including "false" and "true". Letter case does not matter, except for list markers in type on <ol> and <li>. A Vue binding whose value is one JavaScript string, such as :dir="'rtl'", is checked too. Other bound values, component tags, <c-element>, custom elements, elements inside <svg> or <math>, and attributes that take a list of words, such as rel, are not checked. citry check --static and an editor that has not loaded your application report it as a warning unless the component's own Lint class sets the rule as a plain string, because they cannot read your LintSettings.
diagnostics.fix: Use one of the valid values the message lists. For a boolean attribute, write it with no value, leave it out, or bind a JavaScript boolean such as :disabled="saving". If a script on the page reads its own values from the attribute, set rule_invalid_attribute_value to "ignore" for that component.

parameters.attribute: Attribute name as written in the template.
parameters.element: Element name as written in the template.
parameters.value: Attribute value as written in the template.
parameters.allowed: The valid values, quoted and separated by commas.
parameters.suggestion: The valid value closest to the written one.

messages.default: '{value}' is not a valid value for '{attribute}' on <{element}>. Valid values: {allowed}.
messages.suggestion: '{value}' is not a valid value for '{attribute}' on <{element}>. Did you mean '{suggestion}'? Valid values: {allowed}.
messages.empty: '{attribute}' on <{element}> needs a value. Valid values: {allowed}.
messages.target: '{value}' is not a valid value for '{attribute}' on <{element}>. A name that starts with '_' must be one of: {allowed}.
messages.frame-name: '{value}' is not a valid value for '{attribute}' on <{element}>. A frame name cannot start with '_'.
messages.pragma: '{value}' is not a pragma browsers act on in '{attribute}' on <{element}>. If it is an HTTP header, send it in the HTTP response instead. Valid values: {allowed}.
messages.boolean: '{attribute}' on <{element}> is on whenever it is present, so '{value}' still turns it on. Write it with no value to turn it on, and leave it out to turn it off.
messages.boolean-binding: '{attribute}' on <{element}> is on whenever it is present, so the string '{value}' still turns it on. Bind a JavaScript boolean instead, such as :{attribute}="false".

examples.title: An input type the browser does not know
A boolean attribute set to false

diagnostics.title: Misspelled Citry directive
diagnostics.summary: A c-* attribute on an HTML element looks like a Citry directive, such as c-iff for c-if, but is not one, so Citry renders it as an ordinary attribute and the directive never runs. Or a v-* attribute looks like a Vue directive, such as v-iff for v-if, so Vue looks for a custom directive of that name and the page fails.
diagnostics.when: The part after c- is not an HTML attribute that the element accepts, and it looks like a directive: if, elif, else, for, empty, or bind with two neighboring letters swapped, one letter typed twice, or one letter left out, such as c-fro, c-iff, or c-ele; one of those in other letter case, such as c-If; a spelled-out c-elif, such as c-else-if; c-show for c-if or c-model for v-model; or c-key or c-ignore without the #. A different letter, or an extra letter that is not a double, is not a typo, because it usually makes an ordinary word such as c-kind or c-form; neither are c-or, c-bid, c-bin, or a one-letter name. On a custom element, which can define its own attributes, the c-show, c-model, c-key, and c-ignore names are not reported. Only HTML elements, custom elements, and <c-element> are checked, not component tags or elements inside <svg> or <math>. A v-* name is reported on any element outside <svg>, <math>, and v-pre content, component tags included, when it is not a Vue directive and it is a typing slip (two neighboring letters swapped, one letter typed twice, or one letter left out) away from one, such as v-iff, v-shwo, or v-IFF, or is a spelled-out v-else-if, such as v-elif or v-elseif. A custom directive whose name is one slip from a Vue directive is not reported when every component that renders the template registers it in the directives option of $component({...}), under the name as written, its camelCase form, or that form with a capital first letter, such as directives: { iff: {...} } for v-iff or { myDir: {...} } for v-my-dir. Only citry check without --static and an editor that has loaded your application skip it. It is still reported when Citry cannot read that option, and for a directive that a plugin registers with Citry.vue.use(plugin), which no check can see. citry check --static and an editor that has not loaded your application report it too, with the severity the component's own Lint class sets as a plain string.
diagnostics.fix: Use the directive the message names. For a custom directive, register it in the directives option of $component({...}). If the attribute really is meant for the browser, pass it through c-bind, such as c-bind="{'show': value}". For a directive a plugin registers, set rule_misspelled_directive to "ignore" for that component.

parameters.name: Attribute name as written in the template.
parameters.attribute: The attribute name the element renders, without c-.
parameters.suggestion: The directive the author probably meant.

messages.default: '{name}' is not a Citry directive, so it renders an HTML attribute named '{attribute}'. Did you mean '{suggestion}'?
messages.vue: '{name}' is not a Citry directive, so it renders an HTML attribute named '{attribute}'. For Vue's directive, write '{suggestion}'.
messages.vue-directive: '{name}' is not a Vue directive, so Vue looks for a custom directive of that name and the page fails in the browser. Did you mean '{suggestion}'?

diagnostics.title: Misspelled HTML attribute
diagnostics.summary: An attribute on an HTML element looks like a typo of an attribute that element accepts, such as titel for title. The browser keeps it as an unknown attribute and ignores it, with no error.
diagnostics.when: The attribute is not one the HTML Standard lists for that element or for every element, and it is one typing slip from one that is: two neighboring letters swapped, one letter typed twice, or one letter left out, such as titel, clas, or herf. A binding such as :titel, v-bind:titel, or c-titel is checked by the attribute it sets. Letter case does not matter. Names with a hyphen or a colon, such as data-*, aria-*, or hx-*, bindings with a modifier such as .prop, component tags, custom elements, <c-element>, bindings on Vue's <slot>, and elements inside <svg> or <math> are not checked. A c-* name that looks like a misspelled directive, such as c-fro, is reported as citry.template.misspelled-directive instead. citry check --static and an editor that has not loaded your application report it too, with the severity the component's own Lint class sets as a plain string.
diagnostics.fix: Use the attribute the message names. If a script on the page really reads an attribute with this name, write it as data-<name>, or set rule_misspelled_attribute to "ignore" for that component.

parameters.name: Attribute name as written in the template.
parameters.element: Element name as written in the template.
parameters.suggestion: The attribute the author probably meant, written with the same binding prefix.

messages.default: '{name}' is not an attribute of <{element}>, so the browser ignores it. Did you mean '{suggestion}'?

examples.title: A typo in a Vue binding

diagnostics.title: Misspelled HTML element
diagnostics.summary: A tag looks like a typo of an HTML element, such as <dvi> for <div>. The browser renders it as an unknown element with no styles or behavior, with no error.
diagnostics.when: The tag is lowercase, has no hyphen and no c- prefix, is not an HTML, SVG, or obsolete HTML element or one of Vue's built-in tags such as <component>, and is one typing slip from an HTML element: two neighboring letters swapped, one letter typed twice, or one letter left out. Any other unknown lowercase tag is not reported, because a Vue plugin may register a component under that name. Elements inside <svg> or <math> are not checked. Outside <math>, a MathML name one slip from an HTML element, such as <min>, is reported, because there it is more likely a typo of <main>. citry check --static and an editor that has not loaded your application report it too, with the severity the component's own Lint class sets as a plain string.
diagnostics.fix: Use the element the message names. If a Vue plugin registers a component with this name, set rule_misspelled_element to "ignore" for that component.

parameters.tag: Tag name as written in the template.
parameters.suggestion: The HTML element the author probably meant.

messages.default: <{tag}> is not an HTML element. Did you mean <{suggestion}>?

diagnostics.title: Unknown ARIA attribute
diagnostics.summary: An aria-* attribute is not one that WAI-ARIA defines, often because of a typo such as aria-expandd. Browsers and screen readers ignore it, so the element loses the state or label it was meant to have.
diagnostics.when: The attribute name, after any :, v-bind:, or c- prefix, starts with aria- and is not a WAI-ARIA 1.2 or 1.3 state or property. Letter case does not matter. ARIA lets no page invent its own aria-* names, so every unknown name is reported, not only typos. Component tags are not checked, because there the name is an input. citry check --static and an editor that has not loaded your application report it too, with the severity the component's own Lint class sets as a plain string.
diagnostics.fix: Use the ARIA attribute the message names, or the one you meant from the WAI-ARIA list. To keep a custom value on the element, store it in a data-* attribute.

parameters.name: Attribute name as written in the template.
parameters.suggestion: The ARIA attribute closest to the written name.

messages.default: '{name}' is not an ARIA attribute, so browsers and screen readers ignore it.
messages.suggestion: '{name}' is not an ARIA attribute, so browsers and screen readers ignore it. Did you mean '{suggestion}'?
